result.rationale: In sharing mode, parseRefreshTokenResponse uses minimumTokenResponseSchema, which only requires access_token plus bogus computed-key properties ([z.string().toString()] yields a fixed literal key, not a catch-all). Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, so fields like expiry_date returned by the sync endpoint are stripped from the parsed data (e.g. Office365's o365AuthCredentials spread uses only tokenResponse.data). Stale/persisted expiry then keeps triggering refresh on each operation, and each refresh hits CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT and a credential UPDATE — a plausible correctness

judged_text: Sharing-mode refresh amplification: because the broken minimum schema strips the expiry the sync endpoint returns, the stored credential's expiry never advances, so apps that refresh when the stored expiry has passed (Office365, Zoom, etc.) refresh on every calendar/video operation — one POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT plus one credential UPDATE per op on the booking hot path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a new “minimum token response” path via `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, but the finding’s specific claim (“minimum schema strips the expiry so stored expiry never advances, causing refresh on every operation”) is not verifiable from the shown code. In fact, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is defined with computed keys like `[z.string().toString()]`, which will not match arbitrary response keys such as `expires_in`/`expiry_date`; this is more likely to make `safeParse` fail and throw (`"Invalid refreshed tokens were returned"`) than to successfully parse while dropping expiry fields. Also, the code paths shown don’t demonstrate the asserted behavior of repeatedly refreshing solely because an expiry was stripped (and some services still manually set expiry fields before parsing).
